messages.subject: Can find QTLs in scanone but they disappear in mqm
messages.subject_clean: Can find QTLs in scanone but they disappear in mqm
messages.body_plain:
Dear group,

Currently I am involved in studying natural variation for photosynthesis at the Wageningen University.

Recently, I have been studying an F2 population for QTLs that improve photosynthesis efficiency. After the initial F2 mapping, I've found a situation which may warrant mqm mapping to discover the true nature of the QTL.

MQM mapping reads as fulfilling my needs. Using scanone, I find about two to three clear QTL, but they disappear after mqmaugmentation and subsequent mqmscan mapping.

This seems quite odd to me, especially given that in the mqm tutorial (Arends et al 2014), power of QTL should improve. In addition to the tutorial I tested several other of my datasets (which are single chromosome segregating RIL-populations) and in all of these mqmscan improves the power of my QTL.

In this specific F2 population, QTL seem to disappear despite their initial LOD being pretty good - especially for  the size of the population (306).

Is there anyone that could shed a light on how this happens/could happen?

I am willing to share my data.

Thanks in advance!

Roel

messages.subject_clean: Can find QTLs in scanone but they disappear in mqm
messages.body_plain:
Dear Roel,

First off thanks for using MQM, in my experience there is rarely a difference betweeen MQM and scanone.
My first guess would be that the QTL you observe are not additive but dominant QTL.

See if mqmscan(mydata, model="dominance") finds the missing QTLs

Otherwise, I'd like a copy of your data to figure out what is going on.

Kind regards,
Danny

messages.subject: Re: mqmautocofactors() outputs different sets of cofactors, hence different LOD scores, on different runs
messages.subject_clean: mqmautocofactors() outputs different sets of cofactors, hence different LOD scores, on different runs
messages.body_plain:
Deat Nat,

Indeed the autocofactors is a convenience function to place an initial set of cofactors across the genome.
If you get significantly different results, you should build your own genetic cofactors list, and place markers
at locations where you suspect there to be a QTL.

2 approachees:
1) Run different autocofactors runs and build your cofactor list based on which cofactor are not eliminated
2) Another approach I employ is to use scanone and put cofactors at all topmarkers that have a lod score > 2.5, make sure of course that cofactors are not placed within 1 to 2 cM of each other.

Kind regards,
Danny

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] F1 Intercross Maps
messages.body_plain:
I would want to treat such an F1 population from outbred parents as
"4way" (phase-known 4-way cross), but cim() and the mqm functions are
only implemented for backcross and F2 intercross from inbred lines.

 > data(fake.4way)
 > out <- cim(fake.4way)
Error in cim(fake.4way) :
   cim() has not been implemented for 4-way crosses
 > out <- mqmaugment(fake.4way)
Error in mqmaugment(fake.4way) :
   Currently only F2, BC, and selfed RIL crosses can be analyzed by MQM.

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] how to set threshold distance between markers
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] how to set threshold distance between markers
messages.body_plain:
There's not any way to do this. And I'd recommend against trying to estimate the map directly in read.cross().

Rather, read in the data using read.cross(), and then use est.rf(), formLinkageGroups(), orderMarkers(), ripple(), and switch.order(), with a lot of plots in between, to establish the linkage groups and order the markers.

karl

messages.subject: How to tell positive error and ghost QTL?
messages.subject_clean: How to tell positive error and ghost QTL?
messages.body_plain:
Hello Karl,

I recently tried to use multiple-QTL model to do the genome scan manually. I found that one of my traits resulted in four QTLs within 20 cM the manual approach. I think theoretically it is possible, right? But I remembered that I read somewhere in the discussion of this group that finding repeatedly multiple QTLs in a close-by region sometimes is caused by the positive error. So my question is how can we tell whether these QTLs are results of positive errors or the true QTLs?

My second question is how can we tell ghost QTLs in the results of interval mapping? Can multiple QTL scan really detect ghost QTLs? How can we tell whether a QTL is ghost QTL or not?

Thanks!

Ziming

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] How to tell positive error and ghost QTL?
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] How to tell positive error and ghost QTL?
messages.body_plain:
I would look to see where the evidence for the multiple QTL is coming from, or whether it is an artifact. If you drop one or more QTL from the model, how much does the fit change, and why? Evidence for multiple linked QTL must be coming from the individuals showing recombination events between the QTL. How many such recombinants are there, and what do there phenotypes look like?

karl

messages.body_plain:
Ok, so actually the detection of multiple QTLs is basing on the recombination events between the markers. This also means that the missing genotypes, especially the missing recombination genotypes, and the number of markers between the QTLs will affect the detection of multiple QTLs. What about the situation that recombination genotypes of the two QTLs is lethal? Then even if there should be two QTLs, the multiple-QTL scan still can not separate them, because of lacking recombination genotypes. If it is this case, how can we solve this problem?

Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Genetic map
messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl,
